title: Why Doctors Blew Smoke Into People
style: Stylized realistic 3D CGI animation still, high-end animated explainer look, Pixar-meets-realism, cinematic soft lighting, detailed skin, hair and fabric, expressive faces, shallow depth of field, no text, no letters, no gore, vertical 9:16 framing.

sections.name: Why Doctors Blew Smoke Into People

lines.prompt: 18th-century London riverbank at dawn, two men pulling a soaking unconscious man out of the River Thames, a crowd gathering

lines: In the 1700s, if you nearly drowned in London, a rescuer might try to save you with tobacco smoke.

lines.prompt: A wooden kit box opened on the riverbank showing bellows, tubes and a pipe, an 18th-century gentleman lifting the bellows

lines: Kits were placed along the River Thames, with bellows, tubes and tobacco.

lines.prompt: A 18th-century doctor pumping bellows connected to a tube, smoke puffing, the unconscious man covered by a blanket, onlookers shocked

lines: The smoke was blown into the patient, from the other end. Yes, a tobacco smoke enema.

lines.prompt: An 18th-century physician explaining with raised finger to a crowd, glowing warm smoke swirling around a lantern

lines: Doctors believed the smoke would warm the body and get the heart going again.

lines.prompt: A 19th-century scientist in a lab coat dropping a test tube in surprise, pages about nicotine flying

lines: In the early 1800s, scientists showed nicotine is a poison to the heart, and the kits disappeared.

lines.prompt: Modern paramedic in uniform doing CPR on a training dummy on a riverbank, ambulance lights glowing

lines: Today, rescuers use something that actually works. CPR.
